In .NET 6, the new minimal hosting model changes how the host and configuration are built, but you can still read environment variables early in the process.

### How to read environment variables in .NET 6

If you want to read an environment variable **before** the `WebApplicationBuilder` is fully built (for example, to conditionally load configuration files), you can still use:

```csharp
string environment = Environment.GetEnvironmentVariable("ASPNETCORE_ENVIRONMENT");
```

This works exactly the same as in .NET Core 3.1 because `Environment.GetEnvironmentVariable` is a static method available in .NET.

---

### Example: Using environment variable to load configuration in .NET 6

```csharp
var environment = Environment.GetEnvironmentVariable("ASPNETCORE_ENVIRONMENT") ?? "Production";

var builder = WebApplication.CreateBuilder(args);

// Clear default configuration sources and add your own based on environment
builder.Configuration.Sources.Clear();

builder.Configuration
    .AddJsonFile("appsettings.json", optional: false, reloadOnChange: true)
    .AddJsonFile($"appsettings.{environment}.json", optional: true, reloadOnChange: true)
    .AddEnvironmentVariables();

var app = builder.Build();

app.Run();
```

---

### Accessing the environment later

Once the builder is created, you can access the environment via:

```csharp
var env = builder.Environment.EnvironmentName;
```

or

```csharp
var env = builder.Environment; // IHostEnvironment interface
```

But note that this is **after** the builder is created, so if you want to load configuration files based on environment, you need to read the environment variable **before** creating the builder.

---

### Summary

- Use `Environment.GetEnvironmentVariable("ASPNETCORE_ENVIRONMENT")` to read environment variables early.
- Use `builder.Environment` to access the environment after the builder is created.
- The minimal hosting model in .NET 6 does not change how environment variables are read from the OS.

---

If you want to rely on the environment set by the host builder itself, you can also do:

```csharp
var builder = WebApplication.CreateBuilder(args);
var env = builder.Environment.EnvironmentName;
```

But this is only available after the builder is created.

---

**References:**

- [.NET 6 minimal hosting model docs](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/core/fundamentals/minimal-apis)
- [Environment.GetEnvironmentVariable method](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.environment.getenvironmentvariable)

To **exclude filenames that contain forbidden extensions anywhere in the name**, such as `.exe`, `.sh`, `.js`, or `.bat` — even if they appear before the allowed extension like `.pdf` or `.xls` — you need a regex that:

- **Rejects** if any forbidden extension appears anywhere in the filename (not just at the end).
- **Allows** only if the filename ends with `.pdf` or `.xls`.

---

### Problem with your current regex

Your regex:

```regex
([a-zA-Z0-9\s_\\.\-:])(?!(exe|sh|js|bat))+(.pdf|.xls)$
```

- The negative lookahead `(?!...)` only applies to the **next characters** after the current position, not the entire string.
- It doesn't scan the whole filename for forbidden extensions.
- It matches partial strings (like `e.pdf` in `filename.exe.pdf`), which is why it fails.

---

### Correct approach

You want to:

- **Reject** if `.exe`, `.sh`, `.js`, or `.bat` appear **anywhere** in the filename (before the allowed extension).
- **Accept** only if the filename ends with `.pdf` or `.xls`.

---

### Solution: Use a negative lookahead at the start

```regex
^(?!.*\.(exe|sh|js|bat)(\.|$)).*\.(pdf|xls)$
```

---

### Explanation:

- `^` — start of string
- `(?!.*\.(exe|sh|js|bat)(\.|$))` — negative lookahead to **reject** if anywhere in the string there is:
  - `.*\.` — any characters followed by a dot
  - `(exe|sh|js|bat)` — one of the forbidden extensions
  - `(\.|$)` — followed by either a dot (meaning the forbidden extension is in the middle, e.g. `.exe.`) or end of string (meaning forbidden extension at the end)
- `.*` — match any characters (the filename)
- `\.(pdf|xls)$` — ends with `.pdf` or `.xls`

---

### Test cases:

| Filename           | Matches? | Reason                          |
|--------------------|----------|--------------------------------|
| `file.pdf`         | Yes      | Allowed extension, no forbidden |
| `file.xls`         | Yes      | Allowed extension, no forbidden |
| `file.exe.pdf`     | No       | Contains `.exe` before `.pdf`   |
| `file.sh.xls`      | No       | Contains `.sh` before `.xls`    |
| `file.js`          | No       | Ends with forbidden extension   |
| `file.bat.pdf`     | No       | Contains `.bat` before `.pdf`   |
| `filepdf`          | No       | No allowed extension at end     |

---

### Example in JavaScript:

```js
const regex = /^(?!.*\.(exe|sh|js|bat)(\.|$)).*\.(pdf|xls)$/i;

console.log(regex.test("file.pdf"));         // true
console.log(regex.test("file.exe.pdf"));     // false
console.log(regex.test("file.sh.xls"));      // false
console.log(regex.test("file.js"));          // false
console.log(regex.test("file.bat.pdf"));     // false
console.log(regex.test("filepdf"));           // false
```

---

### Summary

- Use a **negative lookahead at the start** to exclude forbidden extensions anywhere.
- Then check the allowed extensions at the end.
- This approach works for filenames with multiple dots and extensions.

---

Searching through 1TB of text data on a local machine with limited resources (dual-core CPU, 8GB RAM) is challenging, but there are definitely ways to speed this up beyond plain `grep`. Here are some practical approaches and recommendations:

---

## Why `grep` is slow here

- `grep` is scanning every file sequentially.
- Disk I/O is the bottleneck — reading 1TB from disk takes time.
- CPU is underutilized because of I/O wait.
- No indexing means every search is a full scan.

---

## Approaches to speed up search

### 1. Use a Full-Text Search Engine (Recommended)

**Tools like [Elasticsearch](https://www.elastic.co/elasticsearch/), [Apache Lucene](https://lucene.apache.org/), or [Whoosh](https://whoosh.readthedocs.io/en/latest/) (Python)** are designed for fast text search over large datasets by building indexes.

- **Index your data once**: This is a one-time cost where the engine parses all files and builds an inverted index.
- **Search is then very fast**: Queries hit the index, not the raw files.
- You can get **file-level metadata** stored in the index, so you know which file contains the match.
- Elasticsearch can run locally, but 8GB RAM and dual-core CPU is on the low side for Elasticsearch. You can tune it to run with limited resources, or try lighter alternatives.

**How to proceed:**

- Write a script to parse each file and index its contents along with the filename.
- Use Elasticsearch or Lucene to perform case-insensitive substring searches.
- You can search for exact strings (not regex) efficiently.

**Pros:**

- Fast repeated searches.
- Scales well.
- Supports complex queries if needed later.

**Cons:**

- Initial indexing takes time and disk space.
- Requires some setup and learning curve.

---

### 2. Use `ripgrep` or `ugrep` instead of `grep`

[`ripgrep`](https://github.com/BurntSushi/ripgrep) (`rg`) and [`ugrep`](https://github.com/Genivia/ugrep) are modern grep replacements optimized for speed:

- Use multiple CPU cores by default.
- Better I/O and memory usage.
- Support case-insensitive fixed-string search.
- Can be faster than `fgrep`.

Example:

```bash
rg -i --fixed-strings "searchTerm" /Folder/Containing/Files
```

or

```bash
ugrep -i -F "searchTerm" /Folder/Containing/Files
```

**Note:** This won't be as fast as indexed search but can be a quick improvement.

---

### 3. Preprocess and Index with SQLite FTS5

If you want a lightweight database approach:

- Use SQLite with the [FTS5 extension](https://sqlite.org/fts5.html) for full-text search.
- Create a table with columns: `filename`, `content`.
- Insert each file's content as a record.
- Build an FTS5 index on the content column.
- Query with `MATCH` operator for fast substring search.

**Example:**

```sql
CREATE VIRTUAL TABLE files USING fts5(filename, content);
```

Then insert data:

```python
import sqlite3
import os

conn = sqlite3.connect('files.db')
c = conn.cursor()

for filepath in all_files:
    with open(filepath, 'r', encoding='utf-8') as f:
        content = f.read()
    c.execute("INSERT INTO files (filename, content) VALUES (?, ?)", (filepath, content))

conn.commit()
```

Search:

```sql
SELECT filename FROM files WHERE content MATCH 'searchTerm';
```

**Pros:**

- Lightweight, no server needed.
- Good performance for moderate data sizes.

**Cons:**

- 1TB of data might be too large for SQLite on 8GB RAM.
- Indexing will take time and disk space.
- You may need to split data or optimize.

---

### 4. Hardware considerations

- **Use SSD instead of HDD**: Disk I/O is the biggest bottleneck. SSDs can speed up scanning dramatically.
- **Increase RAM**: More RAM allows caching and faster indexing.
- **Use multiple CPU cores**: Tools like `ripgrep` use parallelism.

---

## Summary Recommendations

| Approach                 | Speed          | Setup Complexity | Resource Usage | Notes                          |
|--------------------------|----------------|------------------|----------------|-------------------------------|
| Elasticsearch / Lucene    | Very fast      | Medium to High   | Medium to High | Best for repeated searches     |
| SQLite FTS5              | Fast           | Medium           | Medium         | Lightweight DB approach        |
| ripgrep / ugrep          | Faster than grep| Low              | Low            | Easy to try, no indexing       |
| Plain grep               | Slow           | None             | Low            | Baseline                      |

---

## Final advice

- If you want **fast repeated searches** and can invest time upfront, **build an index with Elasticsearch or Lucene**.
- If you want a **quick win without much setup**, try `ripgrep` or `ugrep`.
- If you want a **lightweight DB solution**, try SQLite FTS5 but be mindful of resource limits.
- Consider **hardware upgrades** (SSD, more RAM) if possible.

The function you wrote reverses a `std::strong_ordering` by swapping `less` and `greater`, and leaving `equal` unchanged. Your implementation is correct, but it can be simplified and made more idiomatic.

### Explanation

`std::strong_ordering` is a three-way comparison result type introduced in C++20. It has three possible states:

- `strong_ordering::less` (negative)
- `strong_ordering::equal` (zero)
- `strong_ordering::greater` (positive)

Your function reverses the ordering by turning `less` into `greater` and vice versa, while leaving `equal` as is.

### Simplified version

You can use the fact that `strong_ordering` supports unary negation (`operator-`), which reverses the ordering:

```cpp
#include <compare>

std::strong_ordering reverse(std::strong_ordering v) {
    return -v;
}
```

### Why does this work?

The unary minus operator for `std::strong_ordering` is defined to reverse the ordering:

- `-strong_ordering::less` is `strong_ordering::greater`
- `-strong_ordering::greater` is `strong_ordering::less`
- `-strong_ordering::equal` is `strong_ordering::equal`

This is exactly the behavior you want.

### Summary

Your function can be replaced with a single line:

```cpp
return -v;
```

This is simpler, clearer, and leverages the standard library's built-in operator.

When dealing with coroutines inside a Repository class, **you should avoid using `GlobalScope`** because it lives for the entire lifetime of the application and is not tied to any lifecycle, which can lead to memory leaks or unexpected behavior.

Instead, the best practice is:

1. **Do not create a CoroutineScope inside the repository.**  
2. **Make the repository functions `suspend` functions and let the caller (usually the ViewModel) decide the coroutine scope and dispatcher.**

---

### Why?

- The repository is a data layer component and should be agnostic of threading and coroutine scopes.
- The ViewModel owns the UI-related coroutine scope (`viewModelScope`), which is lifecycle-aware.
- This separation of concerns makes your code more testable and maintainable.

---

### How to refactor your code?

**Repository:**

```kotlin
class ItemRepository(private val itemDao: ItemDao) {

    suspend fun updateItems(itemList: List<ItemDto>) {
        val readDate = DateUtils.getCurrentDateUTCtoString()
        for (item in itemList) {
            item.readDate = readDate
        }
        itemDao.updateItems(itemList)
    }
}
```

**ViewModel:**

```kotlin
class ItemViewModel(private val repository: ItemRepository) : ViewModel() {

    fun updateItems(itemList: List<ItemDto>) {
        viewModelScope.launch(Dispatchers.IO) {
            repository.updateItems(itemList)
        }
    }
}
```

---

### Summary

- **Do not create a CoroutineScope inside the repository.**
- Make repository functions `suspend`.
- Launch coroutines in the ViewModel using `viewModelScope` or other lifecycle-aware scopes.
- Use `Dispatchers.IO` for database operations.

---

### Additional notes

If you really want to create a scope inside the repository (not recommended), you could do:

```kotlin
private val repositoryScope = CoroutineScope(SupervisorJob() + Dispatchers.IO)
```

and then launch coroutines on it, but you would also need to manage cancellation and lifecycle manually, which is error-prone.

---

**In short:**  
**Make your repository functions `suspend` and launch coroutines from the ViewModel's `viewModelScope`.**

Great question! This touches on the subtle topic of object layout and type aliasing in C++.

---

### TL;DR

**No, the C++ standard does *not* guarantee that a trivial struct with a single trivial member has the *exact same* binary layout as that member type itself, even if `sizeof` is the same and there is no padding.**

However, in practice, on all mainstream platforms and compilers, such a struct will have the same layout as its single member (no padding, same alignment, same representation). But this is *not* strictly guaranteed by the standard.

---

### Detailed Explanation

1. **Triviality and layout**

Your `FooIdentifier` and `BarIdentifier` are trivial types (assuming no user-defined constructors, no virtual functions, no base classes, etc.). Triviality means they can be copied with `memcpy`, default-initialized with zeroed memory, etc.

2. **Standard guarantees about layout**

The C++ standard guarantees that:

- The address of the first non-static data member of a standard-layout struct is the same as the address of the struct itself.
- The size of the struct is at least the size of its members plus any padding.
- The members appear in memory in the order of declaration.

But it **does not guarantee** that the struct's representation is *identical* to that of its single member type.

3. **What about padding?**

You already have a `static_assert(sizeof(int) == sizeof(ID_t));` which means no padding at the end.

Also, since the struct has only one member, and it's the first member, the address of the struct and the member coincide.

4. **Is the representation guaranteed to be the same?**

The standard does **not** guarantee that the bitwise representation of the struct is the same as the member's representation. For example, the struct could have some "invisible" padding bits or trap representations (though unlikely for trivial types).

5. **What about `memcmp`?**

Your `memcmp` comparison is comparing the raw bytes of the arrays. If the struct and the member have the same size and alignment, and no padding, then in practice, the bytes will be identical.

But the standard does not guarantee this, so relying on `memcmp` to compare objects of different types is technically undefined behavior due to strict aliasing rules.

6. **Strict aliasing and type punning**

Accessing the bytes of an object through a pointer to a different type (e.g., `char*`) is allowed (since `char*` can alias any type), but comparing objects of different types via `memcmp` is not guaranteed to be meaningful by the standard.

7. **Practical advice**

- On all major compilers and platforms, your approach will work as expected.
- If you want to be absolutely sure, use `static_assert` to check `sizeof` and `alignof`.
- You can also use `std::is_standard_layout` and `std::is_trivial` traits to ensure the type is simple.
- If you want to reinterpret the struct as the underlying int, use `reinterpret_cast` or `std::memcpy` safely.
- Avoid relying on `memcmp` for comparing different types; instead, compare the member explicitly.

---

### Summary

| Property                          | Guaranteed by Standard? | Notes                                  |
|----------------------------------|------------------------|----------------------------------------|
| `sizeof(FooIdentifier) == sizeof(int)` | No (but you check this) | You have a static_assert for this      |
| Address of first member == struct address | Yes                    | Guaranteed for standard-layout structs |
| No padding between struct and member | Yes                    | For single-member standard-layout structs |
| Bitwise representation identical | No                     | Not guaranteed, but practically true   |
| `memcmp` comparison valid         | No                     | Undefined behavior if types differ     |

---

### Example

```cpp
struct FooIdentifier {
    int raw_id;
    // trivial, standard-layout
};

static_assert(sizeof(FooIdentifier) == sizeof(int));
static_assert(alignof(FooIdentifier) == alignof(int));
static_assert(std::is_standard_layout<FooIdentifier>::value);
static_assert(std::is_trivial<FooIdentifier>::value);

int main() {
    int int_array[42] = {};
    FooIdentifier foo_array[42] = {};

    // Addresses of first elements are the same
    assert(reinterpret_cast<void*>(&int_array[0]) == reinterpret_cast<void*>(&foo_array[0]));

    // Comparing raw bytes is not guaranteed by standard, but works in practice
    assert(memcmp(int_array, foo_array, sizeof(int) * 42) == 0);

    // Safer: compare member explicitly
    for (int i = 0; i < 42; ++i) {
        assert(int_array[i] == foo_array[i].raw_id);
    }
}
```

---

### References

- [C++ Standard (draft N4861) - [basic.types]](https://eel.is/c++draft/basic.types#6)
- [C++ Standard - [class.mem]](https://eel.is/c++draft/class.mem#19)
- [cppreference on standard-layout types](https://en.cppreference.com/w/cpp/language/data_members#Standard-layout_types)
- [Strict aliasing rules](https://en.cppreference.com/w/cpp/language/reinterpret_cast#Strict_aliasing)

---

### Conclusion

If you want to create strong typedefs or type-safe wrappers around integers, your approach is fine and will work on all practical compilers. Just be aware that the standard does not *mandate* identical binary layout, so relying on `memcmp` for equality of different types is not strictly portable or guaranteed.

If you want to be fully standard-compliant, compare the members explicitly or use `std::memcmp` only on objects of the same type.

This issue usually happens because of invalid CSS syntax or unescaped special characters in your stylesheets, which the Angular 12 production build (with optimization and minification enabled) is stricter about compared to Angular 11.

### Why does this happen?

- Angular 12 uses a newer version of the build tools (Webpack, CSS minimizers like `cssnano` or `postcss`) that are more strict.
- If your CSS contains invalid characters (like an unexpected `/`), or unescaped special characters, the minifier fails and produces errors.
- The error message about a missing file like `styles.670357240e7c04682d1d.css:9031:1` points to the generated CSS file and line number where the problem occurs, but since it's generated during build, you can't directly edit it.

### How to fix it?

1. **Check your global CSS and component styles for invalid syntax:**

   - Look for stray `/` characters that are not part of comments (`/* ... */`) or URLs.
   - Make sure all comments are properly closed.
   - Check for unescaped special characters in CSS selectors or property values.
   - For example, if you have something like:
     ```css
     background-image: url(/images/bg.png);
     ```
     This is valid, but if you have something like:
     ```css
     content: "/";
     ```
     it should be escaped properly:
     ```css
     content: "/";
     ```
     (This is usually fine, but sometimes complex selectors or content properties need escaping.)

2. **Try disabling optimization temporarily to isolate the problem:**

   Run:
   ```bash
   ng build --prod --optimization=false
   ```
   If this works, the problem is definitely in the minification step.

3. **Use `ng build --prod --source-map` and inspect the generated CSS:**

   - This will generate source maps for your CSS.
   - Open the generated CSS file at the line number mentioned in the error (e.g., line 9031).
   - Look around that line for invalid CSS.

4. **Check your CSS imports and third-party styles:**

   Sometimes imported CSS files or libraries contain invalid syntax that breaks the build.

5. **Try to isolate the problematic CSS:**

   - Comment out large parts of your global styles and rebuild.
   - Gradually uncomment to find the exact block causing the issue.

6. **If you use SCSS or other preprocessors, check their output:**

   - Sometimes SCSS variables or mixins generate invalid CSS if misused.

7. **Update Angular and dependencies:**

   - Make sure you are on the latest Angular 12 patch version.
   - Update `postcss`, `cssnano`, or other CSS-related build dependencies if you manage them manually.

---

### Example: Escaping special characters in CSS

If you have a CSS rule like:

```css
.my-class:before {
  content: "/";
}
```

This is valid, but if you have something like:

```css
.my-class:before {
  content: "/";
}
```

and the build complains, try escaping the slash:

```css
.my-class:before {
  content: "/";
}
```

Usually, the problem is more subtle, like an unclosed comment or a stray `/` outside comments.

---

### Summary

- The error is caused by invalid CSS syntax or unescaped special characters.
- Angular 12 production build is stricter and fails during minification.
- Check your CSS carefully for syntax errors.
- Use `--optimization=false` to confirm.
- Use source maps to locate the problem.
- Fix or escape problematic characters.

Great question! The difference in behavior between `Array.prototype.map` and `Array.prototype.join` when dealing with sparse arrays (arrays with empty slots) comes down to how the ECMAScript specification defines their behavior with respect to *holes* (empty slots) in arrays.

---

### Key points:

- **Sparse arrays** have *holes* (empty slots), which are different from slots explicitly set to `undefined`.
- A slot with `undefined` is a *present* element with the value `undefined`.
- A hole (empty slot) means the property/key for that index does **not exist** on the array object.

---

### Why does `map` ignore empty slots?

The `Array.prototype.map` method internally uses the abstract operation `HasProperty` to check if an element exists at a given index before calling the mapping function.

From the ECMAScript spec (simplified):

1. For each index `k` in the array length:
2. Check if the property `k` exists on the array (`HasProperty`).
3. If it exists, call the mapping function on the value.
4. If it does **not** exist (i.e., it's a hole), skip it and leave the slot empty in the result array.

This means:

- If the slot is a hole (empty), `map` does **not** invoke the callback.
- The resulting array will have holes in the same positions.

Example:

```js
const array = [,,]; // two holes
const mapped = array.map(x => 'x');
console.log(mapped); // [ <2 empty items> ]
console.log(mapped.length); // 2
```

In your example, you see `undefined` because when you print sparse arrays, some environments show holes as `undefined` for convenience, but they are not actual `undefined` values.

---

### Why does `join` treat empty slots as empty strings?

The `Array.prototype.join` method treats holes differently:

- It converts each element to a string.
- For holes (empty slots), it treats them as if they were `undefined`.
- According to the spec, `join` converts `undefined` and `null` to empty strings `""`.
- Therefore, holes are treated as empty strings in the output.

From the spec (simplified):

1. For each index `k` in the array length:
2. If the property `k` exists, get its value.
3. If it does **not** exist (hole), treat it as `undefined`.
4. Convert the value to a string (which for `undefined` is `""`).
5. Concatenate with the separator.

Example:

```js
const array = [,,];
console.log(array.join('x')); // "x"
```

For `[,,,]` (3 holes), you get `"xx"` (two separators between three empty strings).

---

### Is this a documentation problem?

- The MDN docs mention that `join` converts `undefined` and `null` to empty strings.
- They do **not** explicitly mention holes, but the spec treats holes as `undefined` for `join`.
- So, the behavior is consistent with the spec, but the docs could be clearer by explicitly mentioning holes.

---

### Why the difference in design?

- `map` is designed to **skip holes** because holes represent *missing* elements, so the callback is not called on them.
- `join` is designed to produce a string representation of the array, so it treats holes as empty strings to maintain the array length and separator count.
- This difference is intentional and reflects the different purposes of the methods.

---

### Summary

| Method | Behavior on holes (empty slots) | Reason |
|--------|---------------------------------|--------|
| `map`  | Skips holes, does not call callback, resulting array has holes | Holes represent missing elements, so `map` ignores them |
| `join` | Treats holes as `undefined`, converts to empty string `""` | To produce a string with correct separators, holes are treated as empty strings |

---

### Additional note on your example

You wrote:

```js
const array = [,,,];
console.log(array.map(x => 'x')); // prints [undefined, undefined, undefined]
```

Actually, in most environments, this will print:

```js
[ <3 empty items> ]
```

or something similar, because the resulting array from `map` will have holes in the same positions.

If you want to see the difference clearly, try:

```js
const array = [,,];
const mapped = array.map(x => 'x');
console.log(mapped.hasOwnProperty(0)); // false
console.log(mapped.length); // 2
console.log(mapped); // [ <2 empty items> ]
```

---

### References

- [ECMAScript 2023 spec - Array.prototype.map](https://tc39.es/ecma262/#sec-array.prototype.map)
- [ECMAScript 2023 spec - Array.prototype.join](https://tc39.es/ecma262/#sec-array.prototype.join)
- [MDN Array.prototype.map](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/Array/map)
- [MDN Array.prototype.join](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/Array/join)

The difference in behavior between `map` and `join` is intentional and stems from their different purposes:

The issue you're facing is a common one when dealing with the `MANAGE_EXTERNAL_STORAGE` permission on Android 11+ (SDK 30+). Google Play has very strict policies regarding this permission because it grants broad access to external storage, which can be a privacy risk.

### Why is your app rejected?

Google Play **rejects apps that request `MANAGE_EXTERNAL_STORAGE` unless they meet very specific use cases**. This permission is intended only for apps that genuinely need broad file access, such as file managers, backup apps, antivirus apps, etc.

If your app is just exporting CSV files or storing files in your app-specific directories or shared media collections, you **should not use `MANAGE_EXTERNAL_STORAGE`**.

---

### What you should do instead

#### 1. Use **Scoped Storage** APIs (recommended)

Since Android 10 (SDK 29), Android introduced **Scoped Storage**, which restricts how apps access external storage. Apps should use:

- **App-specific directories**: Use `getExternalFilesDir()` to store files that only your app needs.
- **MediaStore API**: For media files (images, videos, audio), use the MediaStore API to save files in shared collections.
- **Storage Access Framework (SAF)**: For letting users pick files or directories.

For exporting CSV files, you can:

- Save files in your app's external files directory (`getExternalFilesDir()`), which does **not require any storage permission**.
- Or, save files in a shared directory using the **MediaStore API** or SAF, which requires user interaction but no `MANAGE_EXTERNAL_STORAGE` permission.

#### 2. Use `READ_EXTERNAL_STORAGE` and `WRITE_EXTERNAL_STORAGE` for SDK < 30

For Android 9 and below, you can still request `READ_EXTERNAL_STORAGE` and `WRITE_EXTERNAL_STORAGE` permissions.

---

### How to fix your app

1. **Remove `MANAGE_EXTERNAL_STORAGE` permission from your manifest** unless your app is a file manager or backup app and you have a valid use case approved by Google.

2. **Update your code to use scoped storage**:

- For exporting CSV files, save them in your app's external files directory:

```dart
import 'dart:io';
import 'package:path_provider/path_provider.dart';

Future<String> getAppExternalDirectory() async {
  final directory = await getExternalStorageDirectory();
  return directory?.path ?? '';
}

Future<void> saveCsvFile(String fileName, String content) async {
  final path = await getAppExternalDirectory();
  final file = File('$path/$fileName');
  await file.writeAsString(content);
}
```

- This does **not require any storage permission** on Android 11+.

3. **If you want to let users pick a directory or file to save to, use the Storage Access Framework (SAF)** via plugins like [`file_picker`](https://pub.dev/packages/file_picker) or [`document_file_save`](https://pub.dev/packages/document_file_save).

4. **If you still need broad storage access (rare case), you must:**

- Declare `MANAGE_EXTERNAL_STORAGE` in your manifest.
- Submit a **Permissions Declaration Form** in Google Play Console explaining why you need this permission.
- Your app must fall under allowed use cases (file manager, backup, antivirus, etc.).
- Otherwise, your app will be rejected.

---

### Summary

| Android Version | Recommended Storage Access Method                          | Permissions Needed                      |
|-----------------|------------------------------------------------------------|---------------------------------------|
| Android 11+ (SDK 30+) | Scoped Storage (App-specific directories, MediaStore, SAF) | Usually **no permission** or `READ_EXTERNAL_STORAGE` for media |
| Android 10 (SDK 29)   | Scoped Storage with legacy flag (not recommended)         | `READ_EXTERNAL_STORAGE`, `WRITE_EXTERNAL_STORAGE`              |
| Android 9 and below   | Legacy storage model                                      | `READ_EXTERNAL_STORAGE`, `WRITE_EXTERNAL_STORAGE`              |

---

### Additional references

- [Google Play policy on `MANAGE_EXTERNAL_STORAGE`](https://support.google.com/googleplay/android-developer/answer/10467955)
- [Android Scoped Storage guide](https://developer.android.com/about/versions/11/privacy/storage)
- [Migrating to scoped storage](https://developer.android.com/training/data-storage/use-cases#opt-out-scoped-storage)

---

### Final note

If your app only exports CSV files, **you almost certainly do NOT need `MANAGE_EXTERNAL_STORAGE`**. Use app-specific directories or SAF instead, and remove the permission from your manifest. This will allow your app to be accepted on Google Play.

The EF Core In-Memory provider is designed primarily for testing and does **not** behave like a relational database. It does **not** support SQL queries, schema manipulation (like renaming or dropping tables), or direct access to the underlying data store via a connection.

### Why you can't do this with the In-Memory provider

- The In-Memory provider stores data in a simple in-memory collection keyed by entity type.
- It does **not** expose a relational database connection or support SQL commands.
- `context.Database.GetDbConnection()` throws because the In-Memory provider is **not** relational.
- There is no concept of tables in the In-Memory provider; entities are stored in memory collections.

### What you can do instead

1. **Manipulate the DbSet directly**

Since the data is stored in memory, you can manipulate the data by working with the `DbSet<T>` directly:

- To "drop" a table, you can clear all data from the corresponding `DbSet`:

```csharp
context.Set<YourEntity>().RemoveRange(context.Set<YourEntity>());
context.SaveChanges();
```

- To "rename" a table is not possible because the In-Memory provider does not have tables or schema.

2. **Use a relational provider for more advanced testing**

If you need to test schema changes like renaming or dropping tables, consider using a lightweight relational database provider such as:

- **SQLite in-memory mode**: supports relational features and SQL commands.
- **LocalDB** or **SQL Server Express** for integration tests.

Example of using SQLite in-memory:

```csharp
var options = new DbContextOptionsBuilder<YourDbContext>()
    .UseSqlite("DataSource=:memory:")
    .Options;

using var context = new YourDbContext(options);
context.Database.OpenConnection();
context.Database.EnsureCreated();

// Now you can execute raw SQL commands
context.Database.ExecuteSqlRaw("DROP TABLE YourTable");
```

3. **Mock or abstract your data access**

If you want to simulate a missing table or schema changes, consider abstracting your data access layer and mocking the behavior in your tests.

---

### Summary

- **No**, you cannot run SQL or rename/drop tables in EF Core In-Memory provider.
- You can clear data from a `DbSet` to simulate dropping a table.
- For schema manipulation, use a relational provider like SQLite in-memory.
- Alternatively, mock or abstract your data access for more control in tests.

The short answer is: **No, you cannot fully omit `TargetFramework` from your project file and rely solely on passing it via the command line for `dotnet restore`.**

---

### Explanation

- The `dotnet build` and `dotnet run` commands accept the `-f|--framework` option, which lets you specify the target framework on the command line, e.g.:

  ```bash
  dotnet build -f net5.0
  ```

- However, **`dotnet restore` does not have a `-f` or `--framework` option**. It relies on the project file to know which target framework(s) to restore packages for.

- When you omit the `<TargetFramework>` or `<TargetFrameworks>` property from your `.csproj`, the SDK tries to infer it, but it fails if it cannot find any framework specified, resulting in the error you see:

  ```
  error NETSDK1013: The TargetFramework value '' was not recognized.
  ```

- This is because NuGet restore needs to know the target framework(s) to resolve the correct package assets.

---

### Why is this design in place?

- The restore operation is decoupled from build and run, and it needs to know the target frameworks upfront to restore the correct assets.

- The `dotnet build` command can override the target framework because it can build for any framework that has already been restored.

- But if you haven't restored yet, the restore step must know the target framework(s) from the project file.

---

### Workarounds / Alternatives

1. **Keep `<TargetFramework>` or `<TargetFrameworks>` in your project file**

   This is the recommended approach. You can specify multiple frameworks if you want to build for multiple targets:

   ```xml
   <TargetFrameworks>net5.0;netcoreapp3.1</TargetFrameworks>
   ```

   Then restore once, and build for any of those frameworks without restoring again.

2. **Use MSBuild properties with `dotnet restore`**

   You can try passing the target framework as an MSBuild property:

   ```bash
   dotnet restore -p:TargetFramework=net5.0
   ```

   However, **this does not work reliably** because the SDK expects the target framework to be defined in the project file for restore.

3. **Multi-targeting with conditional imports**

   You can define multiple target frameworks in the project file and conditionally build for one of them, but this still requires the frameworks to be declared in the project file.

4. **Manual package references**

   As you mentioned, you could avoid NuGet and reference assemblies directly, but this is generally not recommended because you lose the benefits of package management.

---

### Summary

- You **must** specify the target framework(s) in your project file for `dotnet restore` to work.
- You can override the target framework on the command line for `dotnet build` and `dotnet run`, but only after restore has succeeded.
- Passing `TargetFramework` via `-p:` or environment variables to `dotnet restore` is not supported and will cause errors.
- The best practice is to keep `<TargetFramework>` or `<TargetFrameworks>` in your project file.

---

### Example minimal `.csproj`

```xml
<Project Sdk="Microsoft.NET.Sdk">
  <PropertyGroup>
    <TargetFramework>net5.0</TargetFramework>
  </PropertyGroup>
</Project>
```

Then:

```bash
dotnet restore
dotnet build -f net5.0
```

---

### References

- [dotnet build command docs](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/core/tools/dotnet-build)
- [dotnet restore command docs](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/core/tools/dotnet-restore)
- [MSBuild TargetFramework property](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/core/project-sdk/msbuild-props#targetframework)

---

If you want to multi-target, specify multiple frameworks in the project file and restore once:

```xml
<TargetFrameworks>net5.0;netcoreapp3.1</TargetFrameworks>
```

Then build for any framework without restoring again:

```bash
dotnet build -f netcoreapp3.1
```

---

**Bottom line:** You cannot remove the target framework from the project file and expect `dotnet restore` to work without it. The project file must declare the target framework(s).

This is a common point of confusion when working with Azure AD v2.0 endpoint and tokens.

### Key points:

- **Access tokens** issued by Azure AD v2.0 endpoint are meant to be consumed by APIs and typically contain scopes (`scp` claim), not roles.
- **ID tokens** are meant for the client application and contain user identity information, including roles assigned to the user in the app registration (`roles` claim).
- By default, **roles are included only in the ID token**, not in the access token.

---

### Why roles are missing from the access token?

Azure AD v2.0 issues access tokens with scopes (`scp` claim) that represent delegated permissions granted to the client app. The `roles` claim in the access token is only present if:

- The access token is issued for an **API app registration** that defines **app roles**.
- The token is requested with the **correct audience** (the API's App ID URI).
- The user or client has been assigned those app roles.

If you request an access token for Microsoft Graph (or other Microsoft APIs) using scopes like `User.Read`, the access token will contain scopes, not your app roles.

---

### How to get roles in the access token?

1. **Define app roles in your API app registration**

   In your Azure AD app registration (the API), define app roles under **"App roles"** in the manifest or UI.

2. **Assign users or groups to those app roles**

   Assign users or groups to those roles in the Enterprise Applications blade.

3. **Request an access token for your API**

   When you request an access token, the `scope` parameter should be your API's scope, e.g.:

   ```
   api://{your-api-client-id}/.default
   ```

   or

   ```
   api://{your-api-client-id}/MyApp.Read
   ```

4. **Use the correct audience**

   The access token must be requested for your API's App ID URI (audience). If you request a token for Microsoft Graph or other resources, your app roles won't be included.

---

### Example

Suppose your API app registration has:

- App ID URI: `api://1234-5678-90ab-cdef`
- App roles: `MyApp.Read`, `MyApp.Admin`

Your client app requests an access token like this:

```
POST https://login.microsoftonline.com/{tenant}/oauth2/v2.0/token
Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded

client_id=your-client-id
&scope=api://1234-5678-90ab-cdef/MyApp.Read
&grant_type=authorization_code
&code=authorization_code_here
&redirect_uri=your-redirect-uri
&client_secret=your-client-secret
```

The resulting access token will include:

```json
{
  "roles": [
    "MyApp.Read"
  ],
  "aud": "api://1234-5678-90ab-cdef",
  ...
}
```

---

### Summary

- **Roles are included in the access token only if the token is for your API and the user has assigned app roles.**
- **If you request tokens for Microsoft Graph or other Microsoft APIs, roles won't be included in the access token.**
- **ID tokens include roles assigned to the user in the client app registration, but access tokens do not unless the above conditions are met.**

---

### Additional resources

- [Configure app roles in Azure AD](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/active-directory/develop/howto-add-app-roles-in-azure-ad-apps)
- [Access tokens and ID tokens in Azure AD](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/active-directory/develop/access-tokens)
- [How to get roles claim in access token](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/52999294/azure-ad-v2-0-access-token-does-not-contain-roles-claim)

---

If you want to verify the token contents, use [jwt.ms](https://jwt.ms) or a similar JWT decoder.

---

**In short:** To get roles in the access token, request the token for your own API (with app roles defined and assigned), not for Microsoft Graph or other resources.

To include roles in the access token when using Azure AD v2.0, you need to ensure that the API (resource) you're requesting the token for is configured to include roles in the access token. Here are the steps to achieve this:

1. **Define App Roles in the API Application Registration:**
   - Go to the Azure portal.
   - Navigate to `Azure Active Directory` > `App registrations`.
   - Select the API application (the one you are trying to access).
   - Go to the `App roles` section.

Great question! The key to understanding why `stdbuf` doesn't affect Python's output buffering lies in **how Python handles its standard output buffering internally**, and how `stdbuf` works.

---

### How `stdbuf` works

`stdbuf` works by changing the buffering mode of the **C standard library's** `FILE*` streams (`stdin`, `stdout`, `stderr`) **before** the program starts. It does this by using `LD_PRELOAD` to override the `setvbuf` function, so when the program calls `setvbuf` on its standard streams, the buffering mode is changed according to the `stdbuf` options.

This works well for programs that:

- Use the standard C library's buffered I/O (`stdio`),
- And do not override or bypass the buffering behavior.

---

### Why `stdbuf` works for your C program

Your C program uses `printf` (which writes to `stdout`), and the buffering mode is controlled by the C library. When you run:

```bash
stdbuf -oL ./a.out | cat
```

`stdbuf` intercepts the `setvbuf` call and sets `stdout` to line-buffered, so you see the output immediately.

---

### Why `stdbuf` does **not** work for Python

Python's standard output buffering is **not controlled solely by the C library's `FILE*` buffering**. Instead:

- Python uses its own **internal buffering** on top of the OS file descriptors.
- The Python interpreter **does not call `setvbuf`** on `stdout` in a way that `stdbuf` can intercept.
- Python's `sys.stdout` is a **high-level Python file object** that buffers data internally.
- The buffering mode is determined by Python's own logic, which depends on whether the output is a terminal or a pipe, and on the `-u` (unbuffered) flag.

Because of this, `stdbuf`'s `LD_PRELOAD` trick to override `setvbuf` has no effect on Python's internal buffering.

---

### How Python buffering works

- When Python's `sys.stdout` is connected to a terminal, it is line-buffered.
- When connected to a pipe or file, it is fully buffered.
- The `-u` flag forces unbuffered binary stdout and stderr.
- You can also control buffering by using `PYTHONUNBUFFERED=1` environment variable or by manually flushing `sys.stdout`.

---

### What can you do?

- Use `python3 -u` to disable buffering entirely.
- Use `unbuffer` (from `expect`) which runs the program in a pseudo-terminal (pty), tricking Python into thinking it's writing to a terminal, so it line-buffers.
- If you want line-buffering but not unbuffered, you can write a small wrapper in Python that flushes after every line, or use `-u` and manually buffer in your code.

---

### Summary

| Program type | Buffering controlled by | `stdbuf` effective? |
|--------------|------------------------|---------------------|
| C program using `stdio` | C library `setvbuf` | Yes |
| Python interpreter | Python internal buffering | No |

---

### Additional notes

- `stdbuf` only affects programs that use the standard C library's buffered I/O.
- Python's buffering is implemented in the interpreter and is not affected by `setvbuf`.
- `unbuffer` works by running the program in a pseudo-terminal, which changes Python's buffering behavior.

---

### References

- [`stdbuf` man page](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man1/stdbuf.1.html)
- Python documentation on [I/O buffering](https://docs.python.org/3/using/cmdline.html#cmdoption-u)
- Explanation of Python buffering: https://stackoverflow.com/questions/107705/disable-output-buffering

---

**In short:** `stdbuf` cannot control Python's buffering because Python does not rely on the C library's `setvbuf` buffering for `sys.stdout`. Instead, it uses its own buffering logic, so `stdbuf` has no effect. Use `python3 -u` or `unbuffer` if you want to control Python's output buffering.

The reason `stdbuf` has no effect on Python is due to the way Python handles its standard output buffering. `stdbuf` works by modifying the behavior of the standard I/O library functions in C, such as `printf`, `fprintf`, etc. However, Python's standard output is managed by its own I/O library, which does not use the same mechanisms as the C standard I/O library.

In Python, the standard output is typically buffered by the `sys.stdout` object, which is an instance of `io.TextIOWrapper`. This object does not respect the `stdbuf` settings because `stdbuf` modifies the behavior of the underlying C library functions, not the Python I/O library.

To achieve line-buffering in Python, you can manually set the buffering mode of `sys.stdout` using the `io` module. Here is how you can modify your Python script to use line-buffering:

```python
import sys
import io

# Set sys.stdout to line-buffered mode
sys.stdout = io.TextIOWrapper(sys.stdout.buffer, line_buffering=True)

print("input")
while True:
    pass
```

By setting `sys.stdout` to a new `TextIOWrapper` with `line_buffering=True`, you ensure that the output is flushed after every line, achieving the desired line-buffering behavior.

Alternatively, you can use the `PYTHONUNBUFFERED` environment variable to disable buffering entirely, which might be useful in some cases:

```sh
PYTHONUNBUFFERED=1 python3 a.py | cat
```

However, this will result in unbuffered output, not line-buffered output.

In summary, `stdbuf` does not affect Python's I/O because Python uses its own I/O library, which does not interact with the C standard I/O functions that `stdbuf` modifies. To achieve line-buffering in Python, you need to configure the buffering mode directly within the Python script using the `io` module.

You are on the right track with `request.build_absolute_uri()`. Actually, **`request.build_absolute_uri()` does include the query parameters by default**.

Here is how it works:

- `request.build_absolute_uri()` with no arguments returns the full absolute URL including the path and query string exactly as the client requested.
- If you pass a relative path to `build_absolute_uri()`, it will build an absolute URL based on that path, but if you call it without arguments, it uses the current request's full path including query params.

### Example:

```python
def get(self, request, *args, **kwargs):
    full_url = request.build_absolute_uri()
    print(full_url)  # This will print the full URL including query params
    # Use full_url as needed, e.g., for "next page" links
    ...
```

### Why might you have seen it without query params?

If you did something like:

```python
request.build_absolute_uri(request.path)
```

then it would only build the URL with the path, **excluding** query parameters.

### Summary:

- Use `request.build_absolute_uri()` **without any arguments** to get the full URL including query parameters.
- If you want just the path with query params, you can also use `request.get_full_path()` (which returns path + query string, but not the domain).

### Additional info:

- `request.get_full_path()` returns the path + query string, e.g. `/api/items/?page=2&sort=desc`
- `request.build_absolute_uri()` returns the full URL including scheme and domain, e.g. `https://example.com/api/items/?page=2&sort=desc`

---

**So your code to get the full requested URL with query params should be:**

```python
full_url = request.build_absolute_uri()
```

This will give you exactly what the client requested, including all query parameters.

In Django REST Framework, you can get the full request URL including the query parameters using the `request.get_full_path()` method. This method returns the path of the request including the query string.

Here's how you can use it inside your `APIView`:

```python
from rest_framework.views import APIView
from rest_framework.response import Response

class MyAPIView(APIView):
    def get(self, request, *args, **kwargs):
        full_url = request.build_absolute_uri(request.get_full_path())
        # Now you have the full URL including query parameters
        return Response({"full_url": full_url})
```

In this example, `request.get_full_path()` returns the path and query string, and `request.build_absolute_uri()` converts it into an absolute URL.

If you need to construct the URL for the "next page" of results, you can use this method to get the current URL and then modify the query parameters as needed. Here's an example of how you might do that:

```python
from urllib.parse import urlencode, urlparse, urlunparse, parse_qs

class MyAPIView(APIView):
    def get(self, request, *args, **kwargs):
        full_url = request.build_absolute_uri(request.get_full_path())
        
        # Parse the URL and query parameters
        url_parts = urlparse(full_url)
        query_params = parse_qs(url_parts.query)
        
        # Modify the query parameters for the next page
        query_params['page'] = int(query_params.get('page', [1])[0]) + 1
        
        # Construct the new URL with updated query parameters
        new_query_string = urlencode(query_params, doseq=True)
        new_url_parts = url_parts._replace(query=new_query_string)
        next_page_url = urlunparse(new_url_parts)
        
        return Response({"next_page_url": next_page_url})
```

In this example, `urlparse` is used to break down the URL into its components, `parse_qs` is used to parse the query parameters, and `urlunparse` is used to construct the new URL with the updated query parameters.

This should give you the full request URL including query parameters and allow you to modify it as needed for pagination or other purposes.

Great question! This touches on some subtle but important changes introduced in C++20 regarding *implicit object creation* and pointer arithmetic on allocated storage.

---

### Background: Implicit Object Creation in C++20

Prior to C++20, an object was considered to exist only if its lifetime had begun, typically by a constructor call or explicit placement new. Pointer arithmetic and access to elements in raw allocated storage (like from `operator new`) was generally undefined behavior (UB) unless the objects were explicitly created.

C++20 introduced the concept of **implicit object creation** for *implicit-lifetime types*, which includes trivially constructible types and arrays thereof. This means that for such types, the mere presence of suitably aligned storage implicitly creates the object, even if no constructor has run.

---

### Arrays and Implicit-Lifetime Types

- **Array types of implicit-lifetime element types are themselves implicit-lifetime types.**
- For *non-implicit-lifetime* element types (like `std::string`), the array type is **not** an implicit-lifetime type.
- Therefore, an array of `std::string` is **not** implicitly created just by allocating raw storage.

---

### Your Code Analysis

```cpp
void * ptr = operator new(sizeof(std::string) * 10);
std::string * sptr = std::launder(static_cast<std::string*>(ptr));
new (sptr + 1) std::string("second element");
```

- `std::string` is **not** an implicit-lifetime type.
- The array of 10 `std::string`s is **not** implicitly created by the allocation.
- The pointer `sptr` points to raw storage, but no `std::string` objects exist there yet.
- Using `std::launder` here is **incorrect** and leads to UB because `std::launder` requires the object to exist.
- Pointer arithmetic on `sptr` is **not well-defined** because the array object does not exist.

---

### Your Second Example

```cpp
void * ptr = operator new(sizeof(std::string) * 10);
std::string (*sptr)[10] = std::launder(static_cast<std::string(*)[10]>(ptr));
new ((*sptr) + 1) std::string("second element");
```

- Casting to a pointer to an array of 10 `std::string`s is fine.
- But again, the array object does **not** exist yet, so `std::launder` is unnecessary and causes UB.
- Pointer arithmetic on the array pointer is well-defined **if the array object exists**.
- Since the array object does not exist, this is still UB.

---

### The Correct Approach

Since `std::string` is **not** an implicit-lifetime type, the array object is **not implicitly created** by raw allocation. You must explicitly create the array object or its elements.

The standard way:

```cpp
void* ptr = operator new(sizeof(std::string) * 10);
std::string* sptr = static_cast<std::string*>(ptr);

// Construct elements explicitly:
new (sptr + 0) std::string("first element");
new (sptr + 1) std::string("second element");
// ... and so on

// When done, destruct elements and deallocate:
for (int i = 0; i < 2; ++i) {
    (sptr + i)->~std::string();
}
operator delete(ptr);
```

- No `std::launder` needed here.
- Pointer arithmetic on `sptr` is well-defined because `sptr` points to raw storage, and pointer arithmetic on raw pointers is always defined.
- The objects come into existence when you placement-new them.

---

### Summary

| Question                                      | Answer                                                                                  |
|-----------------------------------------------|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Is pointer arithmetic on allocated storage allowed since C++20? | Pointer arithmetic on raw pointers is always allowed, but accessing objects requires them to exist. |
| Is an array of non-implicit-lifetime types implicitly created? | **No.** Arrays of non-implicit-lifetime types (like `std::string`) are not implicitly created. |
| Does implicit creation of such an array create elements? | No, elements are not created implicitly.                                                |
| Is `std::launder` needed or allowed on raw allocated storage? | No, using `std::launder` on storage without an existing object is UB.                   |
| Is pointer arithmetic on a pointer to an array of non-implicit-lifetime types well-defined? | Only if the array object exists. Since it doesn't, it's UB to assume so.                |

---

### References

- [P0593R6: Implicit creation of objects for low-level object manipulation](http://www.open-std.org/jtc1/sc22/wg21/docs/papers/2019/p0593r6.html)
- C++20 Standard, [basic.life] and [expr.add]
- [cppreference on std::launder](https://en.cppreference.com/w/cpp/utility/launder)

---

### Final note

Your **last snippet** is the closest to correct, but **drop `std::launder`** and remember that the array and its elements are not implicitly created. You must explicitly construct each element before use.

```cpp
void* ptr = operator new(sizeof(std::string) * 10);
std::string (*sptr)[10] = static_cast<std::string(*)[10]>(ptr);
new ((*sptr) + 1) std::string("second element"); // OK: pointer arithmetic on array pointer is well-defined
```

But this is still UB because the array object does not exist yet. You should construct elements explicitly and treat the storage as raw memory.

---

**In short:** C++20 does *not* make pointer arithmetic on uncreated objects of non-implicit-lifetime types well-defined. You still need to explicitly create objects before accessing them.

In C++20, the concept of "implicit-lifetime types" was introduced, which allows certain operations on allocated storage without invoking undefined behavior. However, the rules around pointer arithmetic and object creation still need to be carefully followed to avoid undefined behavior.

Let's break down the key points and the code examples provided:

### Implicit Lifetime Types
An implicit-lifetime type is a type for which the storage can be reused without invoking undefined behavior, even if the object has not been explicitly created. This includes types like `std::string`.

### Pointer Arithmetic and Object Creation
Pointer arithmetic on allocated storage is allowed, but it must be done in a way that respects the rules of object creation and destruction. Specifically, you need to ensure that the objects are properly constructed before performing operations on them.

### Code Analysis

#### First Example
```cpp
void * ptr = operator new(sizeof(std::string) * 10);
std::string * sptr = std::launder(static_cast<std::string*>(ptr));
new (sptr + 1) std::string("second element");
```

In this example:
1. `operator new` allocates raw storage for 10 `std::string` objects.
2. `std::launder` is used to obtain a pointer to the allocated storage, but this is unnecessary and can cause undefined behavior because the objects are not yet created.
3. `new (sptr + 1) std::string("second element");` constructs the second `std::string` object in the allocated storage.

The use of `std::launder` here is incorrect because it assumes the existence of objects that have not been created yet. This can lead to undefined behavior.

#### Second Example
```cpp
void * ptr = operator new(sizeof(std::string) * 10);
std::string (*sptr)[10] = static_cast<std::string(*)[10]>(ptr);
new (*sptr + 1) std::string("second element");
```

In this example:
1. `operator new` allocates raw storage for 10 `std::string` objects.
2. The cast `static_cast<std::string(*)[10]>(ptr)` correctly interprets the allocated storage as an array of 10 `std::string` objects.
3. `new (*sptr + 1) std::string("second element");` constructs the second `std::string` object in the allocated storage.

This approach is correct because it respects the rules of pointer arithmetic on arrays and correctly constructs the `std::string` object.

### Conclusion
The second example is the correct way to handle this situation in C++20. It avoids undefined behavior by correctly interpreting the allocated storage as an array and properly constructing the objects.

Here is the correct code:
```cpp
// Implicit creation of an array of std::string, but not the std::string elements:
void * ptr = operator new(sizeof(std::string) * 10);
// The pointer already points to the implicitly created object, so casting is enough
std::string (*sptr)[10] = static_cast<std::string(*)[10]>(ptr);
// Pointer arithmetic on an array is well defined
new (*sptr + 1) std::string("second element");
```

This code correctly allocates storage, interprets it as an array, and constructs the `std::string` object without invoking undefined behavior.

This is a common issue when using Hangfire in development or deployment environments where multiple server instances or old deployments linger and cause confusion about which code version is actually running.

### What's Happening?

- **Old servers keep reconnecting:** Hangfire servers identify themselves by a unique server name (usually a GUID or machine name + process id). When your app starts, it registers a new server in the database. If you have multiple app instances running (e.g., old deployments, leftover processes, or multiple IIS app pools), they all register as servers and pick up jobs.
- **Old code execution:** Hangfire servers execute the code they have loaded in their process memory. If an old server process is still running (e.g., an old IIS worker process, a Windows service, or a container), it will continue to execute the old code even if you redeploy or update your app.
- **Removing servers from the dashboard doesn't kill the process:** Calling `RemoveServer` only removes the server record from the Hangfire storage, but it does **not** stop the actual server process. The server process will re-register itself shortly after, which is why you see old servers come back.

---

### How to fix this?

#### 1. **Stop all old server processes**

You need to ensure that no old instances of your application or Hangfire servers are running anywhere:

- Check your hosting environment for any leftover IIS app pools, Windows services, or containers running old versions.
- Restart IIS or the hosting environment to kill all old processes.
- If running on a server, check Task Manager or `ps` for any lingering processes.
- If using containers, make sure old containers are stopped and removed.

Only after all old processes are stopped, start your new deployment.

---

#### 2. **Use unique server names and monitor server lifecycle**

By default, Hangfire generates a server name automatically. You can specify a custom server name to help identify servers:

```csharp
services.AddHangfireServer(options =>
{
    options.ServerName = $"MyAppServer-{Environment.MachineName}-{Guid.NewGuid()}";
});
```

This helps you track which servers are active and identify duplicates.

---

#### 3. **Configure server heartbeat and server timeout**

Hangfire servers send a heartbeat every 15 seconds by default. If a server doesn't send a heartbeat for 30 seconds, it is considered offline and removed from the dashboard.

If your old servers are not properly shutting down, they might still be sending heartbeats.

You can tune these settings:

```csharp
services.AddHangfire(config =>
{
    config.UseSqlServerStorage(connectionString, new SqlServerStorageOptions
    {
        // Adjust these values as needed
        QueuePollInterval = TimeSpan.FromSeconds(15),
        ServerCheckInterval = TimeSpan.FromSeconds(15),
        SlidingInvisibilityTimeout = TimeSpan.FromMinutes(5),
        CommandBatchMaxTimeout = TimeSpan.FromMinutes(5),
        // etc.
    });
});
```

---

#### 4. **Graceful shutdown**

Make sure your app shuts down Hangfire servers gracefully on app shutdown:

```csharp
public void Configure(IApplicationBuilder app, IHostApplicationLifetime lifetime)
{
    var hangfireServer = app.ApplicationServices.GetService<IBackgroundJobServer>();

    lifetime.ApplicationStopping.Register(() =>
    {
        hangfireServer?.Dispose();
    });

    app.UseHangfireDashboard();
}
```

This ensures the server unregisters itself properly.

---

#### 5. **Avoid deleting Hangfire tables manually**

Dropping Hangfire tables is generally not recommended in production or active environments. It can cause inconsistent state.

If you want to reset the state, do it only in development and ensure all servers are stopped before doing so.

---

#### 6. **Deployments and code changes**

Hangfire executes the code loaded in the server process. If you deploy new code but old server processes are still running, they will continue to execute old code.

Make sure your deployment process:

- Stops old app instances before starting new ones.
- Does not run multiple versions of the app simultaneously unless intended.

---

### Summary

- **Stop all old Hangfire server processes** before starting new ones.
- **Do not rely on `RemoveServer` to kill servers**; it only removes the record.
- Use **unique server names** to identify servers.
- Ensure **graceful shutdown** of Hangfire servers.
- Avoid manual deletion of Hangfire tables unless in a clean dev environment.
- Verify your deployment process **does not leave old app instances running**.

---

### Additional tips

- If you are running in IIS, consider recycling app pools or restarting IIS.
- If you use Windows Services or containers, stop and remove old instances.
- Use Hangfire's **server heartbeat monitoring** to detect stale servers.
- Consider upgrading Hangfire to a newer version if possible (1.7.25 is quite old).

---

If you follow these steps, you should be able to get rid of old servers and ensure only the latest code is executed.

---

**References:**

- [Hangfire Server Lifecycle](https://docs.hangfire.io/en/latest/background-processing/processing-jobs.html#server-lifecycle)
- [Hangfire SQL Server Storage Options](https://github.com/HangfireIO/Hangfire.SqlServer#configuration)
- [Graceful Shutdown in ASP.NET Core](https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/core/fundamentals/host/hosted-services#graceful-shutdown)

Great question! It’s a common point of confusion when first encountering **init-only properties** introduced in C# 9, especially since read-only properties with only a getter (`get;`) and no setter have existed for a long time.

### What you have with read-only properties (`get;` only)

- Properties with only a getter and no setter can only be assigned **inside the constructor** (or inline during declaration).
- After the constructor finishes, the property is effectively immutable.
- You **cannot** assign to these properties anywhere else, including object initializers.

Example:

```csharp
public string Name { get; }  // can only be set in constructor or inline
```

### What **init-only** properties add

C# 9 introduced the `init` accessor, which allows properties to be set **during object initialization**, but nowhere else.

```csharp
public string Name { get; init; }
```

This means:

- You can assign to `Name` **inside the constructor** (just like before).
- You can also assign to `Name` **in an object initializer** when creating the object.
- After the object is fully constructed (after the constructor and object initializer finish), the property becomes immutable.
- You **cannot** assign to it later in the code.

### Why is this useful?

The key difference is **object initializers**.

With read-only properties (`get;` only), this **does not compile**:

```csharp
var thingy = new Thingy { Name = "Test", Description = "Desc" }; // Error: no setter
```

With init-only properties (`get; init;`), this **does compile**:

```csharp
var thingy = new Thingy { Name = "Test", Description = "Desc" }; // OK with init-only
```

This allows for more flexible and expressive immutable types, especially useful in records and DTOs, where you want immutability but also want to use object initializers for convenience.

---

### Summary Table

| Feature                  | `get;` only (read-only)          | `get; init;` (init-only)                  |
|--------------------------|---------------------------------|-------------------------------------------|
| Can assign in constructor| Yes                             | Yes                                       |
| Can assign in object initializer | No                      | Yes                                       |
| Can assign after construction | No                         | No                                        |
| Supports immutability     | Yes                             | Yes                                       |

---

### Example to illustrate

```csharp
class Thingy {
    public string Name { get; init; }
    public string Description { get; init; }
}

class Program {
    static void Main() {
        // Using object initializer - works with init-only
        var thingy = new Thingy { Name = "Test", Description = "This is a test object" };
        Console.WriteLine($"{thingy.Name}: {thingy.Description}");

        // thingy.Name = "Illegal"; // Error: cannot assign after initialization
    }
}
```

---

### Your original class with `get;` only properties

```csharp
class Thingy {
    public Thingy(string name, string description) {
        Name = name;
        Description = description;
    }

    public string Name { get; }
    public string Description { get; }
}
```

- You **must** provide values via constructor.
- You **cannot** use object initializers.
- You **cannot** assign after construction.

---

### Your class with `init` properties

```csharp
class Thingy {
    public string Name { get; init; }
    public string Description { get; init; }
}
```

- You can assign via constructor **or** object initializer.
- You cannot assign after construction.

---

### TL;DR

- **Read-only properties (`get;` only)**: settable only in constructor or inline, no object initializer support.
- **Init-only properties (`get; init;`)**: settable in constructor, **and** in object initializers, but immutable afterward.

This is the main difference and the reason `init` was introduced in C# 9.

---

If you want to allow initialization via object initializers while keeping immutability, use `init` accessors!

This is a known tricky interaction between `position: sticky` headers with inputs and the browser's scroll-into-view behavior when focusing inputs, especially on mobile or some desktop browsers.

Your use of `scroll-padding-top` is the correct modern CSS way to offset anchor navigation so the content isn't hidden behind the sticky header.

---

### Why does the page scroll when typing in the input?

When you focus or type in an input inside a sticky header, some browsers try to ensure the input is fully visible by scrolling the page. This can cause unexpected scroll jumps, especially if the input is near the top and the page is already scrolled.

---

### Can this be fixed with CSS only?

Unfortunately, **there is no pure CSS solution to completely prevent the page from scrolling when typing in a sticky header input** because this behavior is controlled by the browser's internal focus and scroll-into-view logic.

However, you can try some CSS tweaks that may reduce or prevent the unwanted scroll in many cases:

---

### 1. Add `overscroll-behavior: contain` on the header or input

This CSS property can prevent scroll chaining and some scroll adjustments when interacting with elements:

```css
header {
  overscroll-behavior: contain;
}
```

or on the input itself:

```css
header input {
  overscroll-behavior: contain;
}
```

This sometimes helps prevent the page from scrolling unexpectedly when focusing or typing.

---

### 2. Use `scroll-padding-top` on `html` or `body` (you already do this)

```css
html {
  scroll-padding-top: 48px;
}
```

This is correct and should be kept.

---

### 3. Avoid `position: sticky` on the input itself

Make sure only the header is sticky, not the input. Your code is fine here.

---

### 4. Use `touch-action` CSS property (mostly for mobile)

If on mobile, adding:

```css
header input {
  touch-action: manipulation;
}
```

may help reduce scroll jumps.

---

### 5. Use `caret-color: transparent` temporarily (hacky)

Some people try to hide the caret to prevent scroll jumps, but this is not user-friendly and not recommended.

---

### Summary

- Your current CSS with `scroll-padding-top` is correct and should be kept.
- Add `overscroll-behavior: contain` to the header or input to reduce scroll jumps.
- There is no pure CSS way to fully disable the browser's scroll-into-view behavior on input focus/typing inside sticky headers.
- If the problem persists and is critical, a small JavaScript workaround (e.g., preventing scroll on input events) may be necessary, but you prefer to avoid JS.

---

### Example updated CSS snippet:

```css
html {
  scroll-padding-top: 48px;
}

header {
  position: sticky;
  top: 0;
  background: #eeeeee;
  padding: 8px 16px;
  overscroll-behavior: contain; /* added */
}

header input {
  overscroll-behavior: contain; /* optional */
  touch-action: manipulation; /* optional, for mobile */
}
```

---

### Additional notes

- Test on different browsers and devices, as behavior varies.
- If you find the scroll still happens only on some browsers, it may be a browser bug or quirk.
- The related post you mentioned is old; modern browsers have improved but not fully fixed this behavior.
